The Roman senator Meritorius, his brother, his son, and his daughter have varying oratory skill levels. They are seated in rows and columns as shown in the figure with exactly one person sitting in each box. It is known that:

(i) Meritorius' daughter and his brother are seated in the same column.
(ii) His son is seated diagonally across the sibling of the worst orator.
(iii) The best and worst orators are seated in the same row.

Who is the best orator?
questionText: The Roman senator Meritorius, his brother, his son, and his daughter have varying oratory skill levels. They are seated in rows and columns as shown in the figure with exactly one person sitting in each box. It is known that:(i) Meritorius' daughter and his brother are seated in the same column.(ii) His son is seated diagonally across the sibling of the worst orator.(iii) The best and worst orators are seated in the same row.Who is the best orator?
explanationHtml:
Setup: 2x2 grid - Row 1 (C1, C2), Row 2 (C1, C2). Four people: Meritorius (M), Brother (Br), Son (S), Daughter (D).

Clue (i): Daughter and Brother are in the same column.
So {D, Br} are in Column 1 or Column 2 together (one in Row 1, one in Row 2).

Clue (ii): Son is seated diagonally across from the sibling of the worst orator.
The siblings in this group are: Br is sibling of M; D is sibling of S... wait - Br and M are siblings (brothers). D and S are children of M (so siblings to each other).
Worst orator's sibling: if worst = D, sibling = S; if worst = Br, sibling = M.

Clue (iii): Best and worst orators are in the same row.

Working through:
From clue (i): Let D = Row1-C1, Br = Row2-C1 → \rightarrow → M and S fill Row1-C2 and Row2-C2.
From clue (ii): Son is diagonal from worst's sibling. If Son = Row2-C2, diagonal = Row1-C1 = D. D is sibling of Son → \rightarrow → worst orator = Son? But Son can't be diagonal from his own sibling to himself. Try Son = Row1-C2 → \rightarrow → diagonal = Row2-C1 = Br. Br is sibling of M → \rightarrow → worst orator = M.
From clue (iii): Best and worst (M) in same row. M = Row2-C2. So best is also in Row 2 → \rightarrow → best = Br or M. Since M = worst, best = Meritorius' brother

questionText: 'People are crowding around ___ pit into which ___ elephant has fallen. I have never seen an elephant looking more bewildered ___ miserable. Here it is in a most undignified position, thrust into a pit and made to look up ___ a vast, curiosity-stricken crowd.'Choose the option with the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks.
explanationHtml:
Filling the blanks one by one:

Blank 1: '___ pit' - 'pit' begins with a consonant sound → \rightarrow → use 'a' (not 'an')

Blank 2: '___ elephant' - 'elephant' begins with a vowel sound /e/ → \rightarrow → use 'an'

Blank 3: 'bewildered ___ miserable' - connecting two adjectives in a comparison → \rightarrow → use 'and' (coordinating conjunction)

Blank 4: 'made to look up ___ a vast crowd' - 'look up at' is a phrasal expression meaning to gaze upward toward → \rightarrow → use 'at'

Therefore, Sequence: a; an; and; at

questionText: Consider the following statements about four numbers:(S1) The average of the four numbers is 25(S2) Each number is at most 40(S3) Each number is at least 20Choose the option that is necessarily correct.
explanationHtml:
Testing each option:

Option (A): S1 + S2 → \rightarrow → S3?
S1: average = 25, S2: each ≤ 40. Can a number be < 20? Yes - e.g., {5, 30, 30, 35}: avg = 25, all ≤ 40, but 5 < 20. So S3 is NOT guaranteed.

Option (B): S2 + S3 → \rightarrow → S1?
S2: each ≤ 40, S3: each ≥ 20. Average could be anything between 20 and 40. Not necessarily 25.

Option (C): S1 + S3 → \rightarrow → S2?
S1: average = 25, so sum = 100. S3: each ≥ 20.
If one number > 40, say a>40a > 40a>40, then a+b+c+d=100a + b + c + d = 100a+b+c+d=100 with b,c,d≥20b, c, d \geq 20b,c,d≥20.
So b+c+d≥60b + c + d \geq 60b+c+d≥60 → \rightarrow → a≤40a \leq 40a≤40. Contradiction! Therefore no number can exceed 40.

Option (D): S1 → \rightarrow → S3?
Average = 25 doesn't mean each ≥ 20 (e.g., {5, 25, 35, 35}).

Therefore, (C) is necessarily correct.

If the above statement is false, then which one of the following statements is necessarily true?
questionText: 'All the mangoes in the basket are good.'If the above statement is false, then which one of the following statements is necessarily true?

options.html: All the mangoes in the basket are not good.
options.text: All the mangoes in the basket are not good.

options.html: No mango in the basket is good.
options.text: No mango in the basket is good.

options.html: In the basket some of the mangoes are good and some are not good.
options.text: In the basket some of the mangoes are good and some are not good.

options.html: There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.
options.text: There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.

explanationHtml:
Logic analysis using negation of universal quantifier:

The original statement is: 'All mangoes are good' → \rightarrow → In logic: ∀x:G(x)\forall x: G(x)∀x:G(x)

The negation of a universal statement ∀x:P(x)\forall x: P(x)∀x:P(x) is the existential statement ∃x:¬P(x)\exists x: \neg P(x)∃x:¬P(x).

So if 'All mangoes are good' is FALSE, then:
∃x:¬G(x)\exists x: \neg G(x)∃x:¬G(x) = 'There exists at least one mango that is NOT good'

Why other options are wrong:
(A) 'All mangoes are not good' = None are good - too strong, not necessarily true
(B) 'No mango is good' - same as (A), too extreme
(C) 'Some good and some not good' - possible but not necessarily true (could be all bad)

Only (D) is the logical negation that is necessarily true.

explanationHtml:
Analysis of the sentence:
'The team ______ more than 300 runs in 20 overs __________ rains.'

Blank 1 - verb tense:
The sentence is in the past tense (indicated by 'However, some players needed to improve'). The correct past tense form of 'score' is 'scored'. Options using 'scoring' or 'score' are incorrect for a finite verb in past tense.

Blank 2 - conjunction/preposition:
The team scored runs in spite of the rains - showing contrast/adversity. Both 'despite' and 'in spite of' express this. However, 'despite' is followed directly by a noun ('rains'), while 'in spite of' is also followed by a noun - both are grammatically valid here.

'Despite rains' is more concise and natural. Option (C) gives scored; despite.

Option (D) gives 'scoring; in spite of' - 'scoring' is not a finite verb and fails the tense requirement. Therefore, (C) is correct.

Given: P2=Q2+13P^2 = Q^2 + 13P2=Q2+13, where P and Q are positive integers.

(P−Q)(P+Q)=13(P - Q)(P + Q) = 13(P−Q)(P+Q)=13

Step 2: Since 13 is prime, the only factor pairs of 13 are:
13=1×1313 = 1 \times 1313=1×13

Step 3: Set up equations:
P−Q=1P - Q = 1P−Q=1
P+Q=13P + Q = 13P+Q=13

Step 4: Solve:
Adding: 2P=14⇒P=72P = 14 \Rightarrow P = 72P=14⇒P=7
Subtracting: 2Q=12⇒Q=62Q = 12 \Rightarrow Q = 62Q=12⇒Q=6

Step 5: Verify: 72=497^2 = 4972=49, 62+13=36+13=496^2 + 13 = 36 + 13 = 4962+13=36+13=49
